lead: An Euler circuit is a closed walk that uses every edge exactly once. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex exactly once. The two ideas look similar and are often confused. Euler problems ask whether a route can cover every road; Hamiltonian problems ask whether a route can visit every city. Euler has a clean degree test. Hamilton has no simple test, only useful sufficient conditions. The distinction matters in route inspection, delivery planning, circuit testing and tournament scheduling.
prereq: You need: graph vocabulary from 6.1 and paths, cycles and connectivity from 6.3.

blocks.text: An Euler circuit in a connected undirected graph is a closed walk that uses every edge exactly once. It may repeat vertices. The general name is Euler trail: a walk that uses every edge exactly once, closed or open. A closed trail is an Euler circuit; an open trail is an Euler path. A graph with an Euler circuit is called Eulerian. The degree of a vertex is the number of edges incident on it. A loop counts twice.
Euler circuit exists ⇔ every vertex has even degree
blocks.where: The graph is connected and has at least one edge. Degree counts incident edge ends.

blocks.text: The Euler trail test follows. A connected undirected graph has an open Euler path if and only if exactly two vertices have odd degree. Those two vertices are the start and end. If zero vertices have odd degree, the graph has a closed trail, an Euler circuit; some books also count that closed trail as an Euler path. If more than two vertices are odd, no Euler trail exists at all. Adding one edge between the two odd vertices makes the graph Eulerian.

For a directed graph, replace degree by indegree and outdegree. An Euler circuit exists if and only if every vertex has indegree = outdegree and all vertices with nonzero degree lie in one weakly connected component. Weakly connected means the graph becomes connected when edge directions are ignored. An Euler path exists if and only if at most one vertex has outdegree = indegree + 1, at most one has indegree = outdegree + 1, all other vertices balance, and the same connectivity holds.

Hierholzer's algorithm builds a circuit from smaller cycles. Start at any vertex. Follow unused edges until you return to the start; this gives a closed cycle. If unused edges remain at a vertex on the cycle, start another cycle there and splice it into the first. Repeat until all edges are used.

items: Choose any start vertex with degree greater than 0.
Walk along unused edges until returning to a vertex already on the current trail, forming a cycle.
If unused edges remain at a vertex of the cycle, start a new cycle at that vertex.
Splice the new cycle into the old cycle at that vertex.
Stop when every edge is used.

blocks.text: Fleury's algorithm is slower but simple. At each step, choose an unused edge whose removal does not disconnect the remaining graph, unless no other choice exists. Never cross a bridge early. A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the remaining graph. The walk ends when all edges are used. Hierholzer is preferred for programs because it runs in O(E) time for E edges. Fleury can take O(E²) time if bridge checks are repeated.

A Hamiltonian cycle is a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start. A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex exactly once but need not return. A graph with a Hamiltonian cycle is Hamiltonian. Unlike Euler, no simple degree condition decides Hamiltonicity. The general problem is NP-complete.

items: Cut-vertex test: if a graph has a cut vertex, it has no Hamiltonian cycle. Removing that vertex would split the cycle into one path, but the graph splits into two or more components.
Bipartite balance: if a graph is bipartite with parts X and Y, a Hamiltonian cycle needs |X| = |Y|. A Hamiltonian path needs |X| and |Y| to differ by at most 1.
Degree test: every vertex in a Hamiltonian cycle has degree at least 2.

blocks.text: Dirac: n ≥ 3 and deg(v) ≥ n/2 for every vertex v ⇒ Hamiltonian cycle
blocks.where: n is the number of vertices; deg(v) is the degree of vertex v; the arrow means the condition guarantees a cycle, not that every Hamiltonian graph satisfies it.

blocks.text: Ore: n ≥ 3 and deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n for every non-adjacent pair u, v ⇒ Hamiltonian cycle
blocks.where: n is the number of vertices; u and v are distinct vertices with no edge between them.

blocks.text: Dirac is a special case of Ore. Both are sufficient, not necessary. A graph can fail both and still be Hamiltonian. Only a few universities teach the Bondy–Chvátal closure. That method adds edges between non-adjacent pairs with deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n and repeats; if the closure becomes complete, the original graph is Hamiltonian.

figure.caption: Two triangles share vertex C. Every vertex has even degree, so the Euler circuit A-B-C-D-E-C-A exists; C is a cut vertex, so no Hamiltonian cycle exists.

spec.aria: Two triangles A B C and C D E sharing vertex C; every vertex has even degree, so an Euler circuit exists.

examples.question: For the graph with edges AB, BC, CA, CD, DE, EC, list the degree of each vertex and give an Euler circuit. Does Dirac's theorem apply with n = 5?
steps: Count the vertices: A, B, C, D, E, so n = 5. Count the edges: AB, BC, CA, CD, DE, EC, so m = 6.
Count incident edges. A has AB and CA: degree 2. B has AB and BC: degree 2. C has BC, CA, CD and EC: degree 4. D has CD and DE: degree 2. E has DE and EC: degree 2.
All five degrees are even. The graph is connected. By the Euler circuit theorem, an Euler circuit exists.
One Euler circuit is A-B-C-D-E-C-A. It uses AB, BC, CD, DE, EC, CA once each and returns to A.
Dirac needs n ≥ 3 and deg(v) ≥ n/2 for every vertex. Here n/2 = 5/2 = 2.5. A, B, D and E have degree 2, which is less than 2.5, so Dirac's condition fails.

Dirac does not apply. Separately, the graph has a cut vertex C: deleting C would leave two parts {A, B} and {D, E}, while deleting one vertex from a cycle always leaves a single connected path. So no Hamiltonian cycle exists.
examples.answer: Degrees are A=2, B=2, C=4, D=2, E=2; the Euler circuit is A-B-C-D-E-C-A; Dirac's condition needs degree ≥2.5 at every vertex, so it does not apply, and the cut vertex C means the graph has no Hamiltonian cycle.
examples.check:
edges = [('A','B'), ('B','C'), ('C','A'), ('C','D'), ('D','E'), ('E','C')]
deg = {}
for u, v in edges:
    deg[u] = deg.get(u, 0) + 1
    deg[v] = deg.get(v, 0) + 1
order = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']
values = [deg[v] for v in order]
n = len(order)
values.append(n)
values.append(n / 2)
for x in values:
    print(x)

traps: Euler is about edges; Hamilton is about vertices. A graph can be Eulerian but not Hamiltonian, as in the two-triangle figure.
The even-degree test is for a connected graph. A disconnected graph can have all even degrees and still have no Euler circuit.
Dirac and Ore are sufficient, not necessary. Failing them does not prove that no Hamiltonian cycle exists.
For directed Euler paths, balanced indegree and outdegree alone are not enough; connectivity of the nonzero-degree vertices is also required.
A cut vertex rules out a Hamiltonian cycle but not a Hamiltonian path. The figure has no Hamiltonian cycle, yet A-B-C-D-E is a Hamiltonian path.

quiz.q: State the Euler circuit theorem for a connected undirected graph.
quiz.a: A connected undirected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree.

quiz.q: Why does a cut vertex prevent a Hamiltonian cycle?
quiz.a: Removing a cut vertex from a graph splits it into two or more components. Removing one vertex from a cycle leaves one connected path, not two components. So no cycle can visit every vertex and return.

quiz.q: A connected graph has exactly two vertices of odd degree. Does it have an Euler circuit? Does it have an Euler path?
quiz.a: No Euler circuit, because two degrees are odd. Yes Euler path, starting at one odd-degree vertex and ending at the other.

quiz.q: A graph fails Dirac's condition. Can it still be Hamiltonian? Explain.
quiz.a: Yes. Dirac's condition is sufficient, not necessary. A graph may have a Hamiltonian cycle without every degree being at least n/2.

quiz.q: Use the figure graph. Give one Euler circuit. Does the graph have a Hamiltonian cycle?
quiz.a: Euler circuit: A-B-C-D-E-C-A. No Hamiltonian cycle: C is a cut vertex, so removing C leaves two components, which a cycle cannot do.

quiz.q: What conditions must a directed graph satisfy to have an Euler circuit?
quiz.a: Every vertex must have indegree equal to outdegree. All vertices with nonzero degree must lie in one weakly connected component. Then an Euler circuit exists.

quiz.q: Does K₃,₃ have a Hamiltonian cycle? Does K₃,₄ have one?
quiz.a: K₃,₃ does have a Hamiltonian cycle, for example a₁-b₁-a₂-b₂-a₃-b₃-a₁. The balance test alone cannot prove this; it only rules graphs out. K₃,₄ has parts 3 and 4, which are unequal, so by the balance test it has no Hamiltonian cycle.

beyond: Not for the exam. Route inspection, called the Chinese postman problem, adds duplicate edges to make an Eulerian graph and models sweeping every street. The travelling salesman problem is the weighted Hamiltonian cycle problem behind delivery and cab routing. Eulerian ideas appear in genome assembly, where short DNA reads are edges and their order is reconstructed from an Eulerian trail. Search terms: Hierholzer algorithm, Chinese postman, TSP approximation, de Bruijn graph.
